what were impressionist painters actually rebelling against? I know it was a big deal at the time but not why

They were reacting against the strict standards of the official French Academy, which controlled the prestigious Salon exhibitions and favored highly finished, smooth-surfaced paintings of historical, mythological, or religious subjects, typically composed and painted carefully in a studio rather than outdoors. Painters like Monet, Renoir, and Degas instead wanted to capture fleeting, everyday moments and the actual sensory experience of light and atmosphere as it changed from minute to minute, which pushed them to paint outdoors, a practice called en plein air, often working quickly with visible, loose brushstrokes and unmixed colors placed side by side rather than smoothly blended, letting the viewer's eye do some of the optical blending. This was considered radical and unfinished-looking by Academy standards, and their unofficial exhibitions, held independently after the Academy repeatedly rejected their work, were initially mocked by critics, with the term impressionism itself originating as a somewhat derisive reference to Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, implying the work looked like a rough sketch rather than a completed piece.
did the Academy's rejection actually hurt their careers financially at the time or did they do okay?

It took roughly a couple of decades before Impressionism moved from being ridiculed to being commercially successful and critically respected, and by the later part of their careers many of the major Impressionists, particularly Monet, did become quite financially successful, but that reversal came only after a long stretch of being considered outsiders by the mainstream art establishment.

I keep getting confused about the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL. I understand them individually when I look them up but I can't seem to keep it straight when actually writing queries. Any way to make this click permanently?

The stickiest way to internalize this is a visual/set mental model rather than memorizing definitions, since the definitions themselves are what keeps slipping out of memory. Picture two overlapping circles, a Venn diagram, one circle for table A, one for table B, overlapping in the middle where rows match on your join condition. INNER JOIN returns only the overlapping middle section, rows that have a match in both tables, anything in either table without a match on the other side is simply dropped entirely, gone from the result. LEFT JOIN returns the entire left circle, all of table A no matter what, plus the overlapping middle where matches exist, but where table A has no match in table B, those columns from B just show up as NULL rather than the row being dropped, this is the key difference from inner join, nothing from the left table ever disappears. FULL OUTER JOIN returns the entire combined area of both circles, everything from A, everything from B, with NULLs filling in wherever a match doesn't exist on the other side, so unlike inner join, nothing from either table is ever dropped. A memory trick that helps a lot of people: with LEFT JOIN, read it as "give me everything from the left table, and whatever matches from the right, it's fine if there's nothing on the right." That plain English framing tends to stick better than the Venn diagram alone once you pair the two together.
That helps. When would I actually want a LEFT JOIN over an INNER JOIN in a real scenario, not just conceptually?

The real world signal for choosing LEFT JOIN over INNER JOIN is whenever the absence of a match is itself meaningful information you want to see in your results, rather than something you're fine silently discarding. A classic example: imagine a customers table and an orders table, and you want a report of all customers along with their most recent order. If you use INNER JOIN, any customer who has never placed an order simply vanishes from your results entirely, which is a problem if your actual goal was something like "show me all customers, including ones who haven't ordered yet, so marketing can target them with a promotion." A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders keeps every customer in the result regardless of whether they have orders, with NULL values in the order columns for customers with no orders, which you can then filter for directly, like WHERE order_id IS NULL, to specifically identify customers who've never purchased anything, a query that's structurally impossible to write correctly using INNER JOIN since those rows wouldn't exist in an inner-joined result to filter in the first place. As a general rule of thumb: use INNER JOIN when you only care about complete, matched records, like a sales report that only makes sense for actual transactions that happened, and reach for LEFT JOIN whenever one side of the relationship is your "primary" entity you want fully preserved regardless of whether a related record exists, like customers, employees, or products where the absence of related activity is meaningful business information.
quick refresher - what's actually the difference between the light and dark reactions in photosynthesis?

The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membrane and require light directly - chlorophyll absorbs photons, which drives electron transport chains that split water and release oxygen, generate ATP, and produce NADPH. The light-independent reactions, commonly called the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma and use that ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into organic molecules like G3P, which eventually gets built into glucose. The dark reactions name is a bit misleading since it doesn't literally require darkness - it just doesn't need light directly, though it depends on the products of the light reactions to run.
so if you cut off CO2 but kept the light on, what would happen to the cycle?

The Calvin cycle would stall pretty quickly because RuBisCO has no substrate to fix carbon onto. ATP and NADPH would keep piling up from the light reactions with nowhere to be used, which would eventually feed back and slow the light reactions too, since NADP+ wouldn't be regenerated fast enough. In experiments, this kind of CO2 deprivation is actually used to study Calvin cycle intermediates - you can watch levels of compounds like RuBP and 3-PGA shift as the cycle backs up without carbon input.

what's actually happening in the brain during REM sleep that's different from deep sleep?

During REM sleep, brain activity as measured by EEG looks surprisingly similar to wakefulness - fast, low-amplitude waves - even though the body is in a state of near-total muscle paralysis called atonia, which is thought to prevent you from physically acting out dreams. This is when most vivid, narrative dreaming occurs, and areas like the amygdala and visual association cortex show high activity while the prefrontal cortex, involved in logic and self-control, is relatively less active, which may explain why dreams often feel emotionally intense but logically bizarre. Deep sleep, or slow-wave sleep, is almost the opposite pattern - large, slow, synchronized delta waves dominate, muscle tone is largely intact, and this stage is associated more with physical restoration, growth hormone release, and consolidation of declarative memory rather than vivid dreaming.
why does the body paralyze itself specifically during REM and not during other stages?

It's driven by specific brainstem circuits, particularly in the pons, that become active during REM and send inhibitory signals down the spinal cord to motor neurons, effectively cutting off voluntary muscle activation. Researchers think this evolved specifically because REM is when the brain is generating vivid, motor-command-like dream content, so without that inhibition you'd be at risk of physically thrashing around or acting out whatever's happening in the dream. This is actually demonstrated clearly in a condition called REM sleep behavior disorder, where that inhibitory circuit fails and people physically act out their dreams, sometimes violently, which is strong evidence for why the paralysis mechanism exists in the first place.
how did scholars actually manage to translate hieroglyphics if nobody had spoken the language in centuries?

The breakthrough came from the Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, which had the same decree inscribed in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, an everyday Egyptian script, and ancient Greek, which scholars could already read fluently. Because the Greek text gave a known reference translation, scholars could work out that the hieroglyphic and Demotic versions said the same thing, and use the Greek as a key to start matching specific hieroglyphic symbols to known words and names. Jean-Francois Champollion made the decisive breakthrough in the 1820s by focusing on cartouches, the oval rings enclosing royal names, correctly guessing that the hieroglyphs inside spelled out the name Ptolemy phonetically, and cross-referencing that with a similarly enclosed name he identified as Cleopatra on a different inscription, which let him confirm that certain hieroglyphic signs functioned phonetically, representing sounds, rather than purely as ideograms representing whole concepts or objects, which had been the dominant assumption before that.
so hieroglyphics are a mix of phonetic symbols and picture-symbols then, not purely one or the other?

Exactly, and that mixed nature is part of why earlier attempts to decode it purely as a symbolic picture-language kept failing. Egyptian hieroglyphic writing combines phonograms, symbols representing individual sounds or sound combinations, with logograms representing whole words or concepts directly, and determinatives, additional symbols placed at the end of a word with no phonetic value themselves but clarifying which category of meaning the word belongs to, helping distinguish between homophones. Champollion's insight was recognizing that the system used phonetic elements extensively, especially for foreign names like Ptolemy and Cleopatra that had no pre-existing traditional logogram, which forced the scribes to spell them out sound by sound using phonetic hieroglyphs, giving him the crack he needed into the system as a whole.

I have a short story about two estranged sisters who reconnect at their mother's funeral, but I don't know how to end it. Don't want it too sappy or too bleak.

A middle-ground ending usually works best with something small and unresolved-but-hopeful rather than a full reconciliation or a full rupture. A few options: end on a small shared gesture that implies more than it states — one sister handing the other something of their mother's without a big speech, or the two of them doing an ordinary task together (packing up a kitchen, driving somewhere) where the silence between them is easier than it was at the start, even if nothing is explicitly 'fixed.' You could also end mid-conversation, cutting away right as one of them starts to say something real, which lets the reader feel the door open without you having to write the whole reconciliation. The key move for avoiding both sappy and bleak is restraint — let the gesture or detail carry the emotional weight instead of a character stating how they feel.
I like the idea of ending mid-conversation. Any risk that feels like a cop-out to readers?

It can read as a cop-out if it's the story's only unresolved thread and the cut feels abrupt with no groundwork. It reads as intentional, though, if you've been building toward that specific moment (the reader can feel it coming) and if the rest of the story's tensions — not just the sisters' relationship, but any other threads — are otherwise resolved enough that this one open thread feels like a deliberate choice rather than the story simply running out of pages. One trick: give the line right before the cut some weight of its own, so even without hearing what comes next, the reader has something to sit with.

Spin both wheels and check they're true (not wobbling side to side) and that brakes engage smoothly without excessive rubbing. Test all the gears by shifting through the full range while pedaling, listening for grinding or the chain skipping. Check tire tread and sidewalls for cracking, and squeeze the brakes to make sure pads have decent life left. Also just take it for a short ride if the seller allows, since some issues (headset looseness, bottom bracket play) are easier to feel than see.
how do I check if it's actually the right size for me before buying

Once on the bike, with the pedal at its lowest point, your leg should be almost fully extended with a slight bend at the knee, not locked straight. Reaching the handlebars shouldn't feel like you're stretching uncomfortably or hunched too far forward. If the seller lets you test ride it, pay attention to whether you feel cramped or overextended after a few minutes, that's usually the clearest sign the size is off even if the standover height seemed fine at first.

I'm still fairly new to git and merge conflicts genuinely terrify me, I usually just ask a teammate to fix them for me. Can you explain what's actually happening during a conflict and how to resolve one myself without breaking everything?

That fear is really common early on and it's worth understanding that a merge conflict is actually a pretty safe situation, git is explicitly pausing and asking you for help specifically because it wants to avoid silently making a wrong guess about your code, it's a safety feature, not a sign something has already gone badly wrong. Here's what's actually happening: when you merge or pull changes, git tries to automatically combine changes from two different branches line by line. Most of the time this works silently since changes usually touch different parts of a file. A conflict happens specifically when both branches changed the exact same lines (or very nearby lines) in different ways, and git has no reasonable way to guess which version you actually want, or whether you want some combination of both, so it stops and hands the decision to you rather than guessing wrong. When you open a conflicted file, git marks the conflicting section with specific markers: <<<<<<< HEAD shows the start of your current branch's version, a line of ======= separates the two versions, and >>>>>>> branch-name marks the end of the incoming branch's version. Your job is simply to look at both versions, decide what the final correct code should be (keep yours, keep theirs, or hand-write a combination of both), delete the marker lines themselves along with whichever version(s) you don't want, save the file, then stage it with git add and continue the merge, either git commit for a merge conflict or git rebase --continue for a rebase conflict.
That actually helps a lot, it sounds less scary framed that way. Is there anything I can do beforehand to reduce how often I even run into conflicts in the first place?

Yes, a few habits meaningfully reduce conflict frequency, and they're mostly about reducing how long your branch diverges from everyone else's changes before you reconcile, since conflict likelihood scales pretty directly with how much unmerged change has piled up on both sides simultaneously. First and most impactful: pull or merge the main branch into your feature branch frequently, ideally daily if you're working on a multi-day feature, rather than working in isolation for a week and then trying to merge everything at once, since a week's worth of accumulated changes from teammates dramatically increases the odds of overlapping edits, while frequent small merges mean you resolve tiny conflicts (or none at all) regularly instead of one large, scary one at the end. Second, keep your branches and commits focused and short-lived where possible, a feature branch that lives for two days touching a handful of files is inherently lower conflict risk than one that lives for three weeks touching dozens of files across the whole codebase, since more surface area and more time both increase overlap odds. Third, communicate with teammates about who's touching what, especially for shared files that everyone tends to modify (a main config file, a shared utility file, a central routes file), a quick heads up in chat before starting work on a commonly-contested file often prevents conflicts entirely rather than needing to resolve them after the fact. Finally, commit and push in smaller, more frequent increments rather than one giant commit at the end of a work session, smaller commits make any conflict that does occur much easier to reason about, since you're comparing a small, focused change rather than untangling one enormous commit touching many unrelated things at once.

why do my succulents keep dying, I water them all the time to be safe

That's actually the problem, succulents store water in their leaves and are adapted to dry, infrequent watering, so "watering a lot to be safe" is the opposite of what they need. Overwatering leads to root rot, which often looks like mushy, translucent, or yellowing leaves, easy to mistake for underwatering at first glance which makes people water even more.

Depends on the species and pot/soil, but a good general approach is to let the soil dry out completely between waterings, then water thoroughly until it drains out the bottom. In most homes that ends up being every 2-3 weeks, sometimes longer in winter when they're semi-dormant. Stick a finger in the soil before watering rather than following a fixed schedule, and make sure the pot has drainage holes since standing water is what actually causes the rot.
our team keeps arguing about rebase vs merge for feature branches. what's actually the tradeoff

Merge preserves the true history of what happened - you get a merge commit that shows exactly when and how a branch was integrated, and it never rewrites commits that have already been pushed, which makes it safer for shared branches. The downside is your history can get cluttered with lots of merge commits and a tangled-looking graph if many people are merging frequently. Rebase rewrites your branch's commits so they appear to start from the current tip of the target branch, producing a linear history that's easier to read and bisect. The tradeoff is that it rewrites commit hashes, so if you rebase a branch that others have already pulled and built on top of, you create divergent histories and a mess of duplicate commits when they try to sync up. The common compromise a lot of teams land on is: rebase freely on your own local, not-yet-pushed feature branch to clean it up before opening a PR, but never rebase shared branches, and use merge or squash-merge when actually integrating into main.
what's squash merge do differently from a regular merge then

Squash merge takes all the commits on your feature branch and condenses them into a single new commit on the target branch, discarding the individual commit boundaries though the diff content is preserved. It's popular because it keeps main's history to one tidy commit per feature, regardless of how messy or exploratory the commits on the branch were. The tradeoff is you lose the fine-grained commit-by-commit history if you ever want to bisect within that feature's development - from main's perspective it's just one atomic change.
I'm 34 and never learned to swim properly, I can sort of doggy paddle to survive but that's it. Is it realistic to actually learn proper swimming as an adult, and how would I even start?

It's completely realistic, and honestly adult swim learners often progress faster in some respects than children do, since you can understand and apply verbal instruction and body mechanics concepts that young kids simply can't process yet, the common belief that swimming is something you need to learn young or not at all is largely a myth, plenty of adults learn from scratch successfully every year. The biggest initial hurdle for most adult beginners isn't physical, it's psychological, specifically water comfort and breath control anxiety, so a good starting approach prioritizes comfort before any actual stroke technique. I'd strongly recommend adult-specific swim lessons rather than trying to self-teach from videos initially, most pools and community centers offer these specifically because adult beginners have different needs and anxieties than a kids' class structure addresses, and having an instructor in the water physically supporting you initially removes a lot of the fear that makes self-teaching much harder. The typical progression: first sessions focus purely on water comfort, floating, controlled breathing with your face in the water, and basic kicking while holding the wall or a kickboard, no actual stroke yet. Once floating and breath control feel manageable, usually after several sessions, freestyle stroke mechanics get introduced piece by piece, arm pull, then breathing rhythm, then combining them, rather than all at once, which is where most self-taught attempts go wrong, trying to coordinate everything simultaneously from day one.
The breathing/face in the water part is honestly what scares me the most. Any specific tips for getting past that fear?

That fear is extremely common, arguably the single most common barrier for adult beginners specifically, and it responds really well to a very gradual, self-paced exposure approach rather than forcing it all at once, so don't feel discouraged if it takes longer than the rest of the process, that's completely normal and expected. Start in shallow water where you can stand comfortably at any moment, this control matters enormously for anxiety, knowing you can stand up instantly removes a huge portion of the fear response. First step, before even submerging your face, just practice exhaling slowly through your nose and mouth while standing with water at chin level, getting comfortable with the sensation of controlled breath near water. Next, practice just dipping your chin and mouth (not full face) into the water while blowing bubbles gently, holding the wall for security, for just a second or two at a time, gradually increasing duration as it feels more natural. Once that's comfortable, progress to fully submerging your face for just 1-2 seconds while blowing bubbles, then coming back up, repeating this many times rather than trying to hold it longer each time, repetition at a comfortable duration builds confidence faster than pushing duration too soon. A specific technique that helps a lot of anxious adult swimmers: practice this rhythm, exhale slowly and completely through your nose while your face is submerged, then lift your head to inhale through your mouth, this exhale-underwater, inhale-above-water rhythm is the actual mechanic you're building toward for real stroke breathing anyway, so this "scary" practice is directly building the skill you need later, not just separate fear exposure. Most adult learners report this specific fear easing substantially within 3-5 practice sessions of this gradual approach, even when other aspects of swimming click faster.

I started keto about 2 weeks ago and I have zero energy, headaches, kind of foggy. Is this normal or did I mess something up?

What you're describing sounds very consistent with what's commonly called "keto flu," a cluster of symptoms, fatigue, headache, brain fog, sometimes irritability or nausea, that a lot of people experience in the first one to two weeks of a ketogenic diet, so this is a known and common experience, not necessarily a sign you've done something wrong, though there are a couple of likely specific causes worth addressing directly rather than just waiting it out passively. The primary driver is usually electrolyte imbalance, specifically sodium, potassium, and magnesium, when you drastically cut carbs, your body's insulin levels drop significantly, and lower insulin causes your kidneys to excrete more sodium (and water) than usual, which then also pulls potassium and magnesium out along with it, this electrolyte depletion is what's actually behind most of the fatigue, headache, and fogginess, much more than "your body adjusting to fat burning" as it's sometimes casually described. The direct fix: significantly increase your sodium intake, more than feels intuitive, many keto guides recommend somewhere around 3000-5000mg of sodium daily during this adjustment period, which is well above typical dietary guidelines but appropriate given how much you're now excreting, adding broth, salting food more liberally than usual, or even a plain glass of water with a measured amount of salt dissolved in it can meaningfully help within hours, not days. Also actively supplement potassium-rich foods like avocado and leafy greens, and consider a magnesium supplement, since these three electrolytes together typically resolve the bulk of keto flu symptoms within a day or two of correcting for them properly.
How do I know if it's actually electrolytes versus just not eating enough calories overall? I've also cut portions a bit without really meaning to.

That's a smart distinction to draw, since the two causes have overlapping symptoms but somewhat different fixes, and it's genuinely common for both to be happening simultaneously when someone starts keto, since cutting out an entire food category often unintentionally reduces overall intake too, especially if you haven't consciously replaced those calories with adequate fat and protein. A few ways to tell them apart. Timing and pattern: electrolyte-related fatigue tends to feel more acute and symptom-specific, headaches, muscle cramps or twitches, dizziness on standing up quickly (a classic sign of low sodium specifically), while general caloric insufficiency tends to feel more like persistent, flat low energy and increased hunger or preoccupation with food throughout the day, without necessarily the more acute headache or dizziness component. The most reliable way to actually distinguish them rather than guessing is simply to track for a few days, honestly log what you're eating including approximate calories, and separately track your sodium intake specifically, most people significantly underestimate both how few calories they're eating and how little sodium they're getting once they cut processed foods, which often contain a lot of hidden sodium, without deliberately compensating. Given that you mentioned unintentionally cutting portions, I'd address both simultaneously rather than trying to isolate one cause first: increase sodium as described, and separately make sure you're eating enough total food, keto specifically requires eating adequately from fat and protein sources to replace the calories that carbs used to provide, if you've simply removed carbs without adding more fat and protein to compensate, you've accidentally created a low-calorie diet on top of a ketogenic one, which compounds fatigue considerably. Aim to eat until genuinely satisfied at meals rather than restricting further, fattier cuts of meat, added oils, nuts, and full-fat dairy are all appropriate and expected to be eaten more liberally on keto specifically to prevent this exact accidental under-eating problem.
